title: Missingness Bias Calibration in Feature Attribution Explanations
claim: Removing irrelevant inputs can flip a correct model prediction to a wrong one, exposing a bias from ablated, out-of-distribution inputs.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, each with predicted-label checkmark or cross below
description: Three brain MRI images sit side by side, each with a predicted label underneath. The left panel is the clean scan. It shows a dark tumor, marked by a red arrow, and is labeled 'Tumor' with a green checkmark. The middle panel keeps only a subset of relevant patches. The patches are the skull region and part of the tumor. The rest is covered by teal-and-gray diagonal stripes, which mark masked, zero-valued pixels. It is also labeled 'Tumor' with a green checkmark. The right panel masks a different set of regions, apparently the irrelevant ones, and leaves the tumor visible. It is labeled 'Healthy' with a red cross. The eye goes first to the left MRI and its red arrow, then follows the progressive masking to the red cross on the right. The figure uses little text and strong visual contrast.
caption: Removing irrelevant features can cause a misdiagnosis. A fine-tuned ViT [ref] correctly predicts "tumor" on the clean image (left) and a subset of the relevant features (middle). However, masking irrelevant features flips the prediction to "healthy", despite the tumor remaining visible (right). For visualization, gray stripes denote zero-valued pixels, and images are contrast-boosted.
abstract: Popular explanation methods often produce unreliable feature importance scores due to missingness bias, a systematic distortion that arises when models are probed with ablated, out-of-distribution inputs. Existing solutions treat this as a deep representational flaw that requires expensive retraining or architectural modifications. In this work, we challenge this assumption and show that missingness bias can be effectively treated as a superficial artifact of the model's output space. We introduce MCal, a lightweight post-hoc method that corrects this bias by fine-tuning a simple linear head on the outputs of a frozen base model. Surprisingly, we find this simple correction consistently reduces missingness bias and is competitive with, or even outperforms, prior heavyweight approaches across diverse medical benchmarks spanning vision, language, and tabular domains.
